args.query: What is the role and function of the learnable class token in ViT?
In DeiT's distillation-token procedure, which target trains the class branch and which target trains the distillation branch?
How does DeiT's late-fusion inference combine the class-branch and distillation-branch outputs?

args.instructions: Answer the question directly in the first sentence. Then compare what each paper says, naming the paper for every point, and state where the papers agree, disagree or report numbers that are not comparable. If one hop of the question is not answered by the evidence, say which.

result.answer:
Answer: In ViT, the learnable [class] token is taken as the image representation and its output is converted into the class prediction; in DeiT, the class branch is trained against the true label, the distillation branch against the teacher's hard predicted label, and late-fusion inference adds the two classifiers' softmax outputs.

The ViT paper (2010.11929v2) says an additional [class] token is taken as the image representation, and that this token's output is transformed into a class prediction by a small MLP with tanh nonlinearity in its single hidden layer [S:2ec4ef3fa836#117]. It also says this [class]-token design is inherited from the text Transformer and is used throughout the main paper [S:2ec4ef3fa836#118]. The DeiT paper (2012.12877v2) describes the class token as a trainable vector appended to the patch tokens before the first layer, passing through the transformer layers and then being projected with a linear layer to predict the class [S:4cebd2b97b41#23]; it adds that only the class vector is used to predict the output, forcing self-attention to spread information between the patch tokens and the class token, with training supervision coming only from the class embedding while patch tokens are the only variable input [S:4cebd2b97b41#23]. The papers agree on the class token's role as the image-level representation used for classification; their head descriptions differ: ViT describes a small MLP with tanh [S:2ec4ef3fa836#117], whereas DeiT describes a linear layer [S:4cebd2b97b41#23] and says it does not use an MLP head for pre-training but only a linear classifier [S:4cebd2b97b41#34].

For DeiT's distillation procedure, the distillation token's output objective is to reproduce the teacher's (hard) predicted label instead of the true label [S:4cebd2b97b41#28], and its target objective is given by the distillation component of the loss [S:4cebd2b97b41#29]. Thus the class branch is trained against the true label, while the distillation branch is trained against the teacher's hard predicted label [S:4cebd2b97b41#28]. At test time both the class and distillation embeddings have linear classifiers and can infer the image label, but DeiT's referent late-fusion method adds the softmax outputs of the two classifiers to make the prediction [S:4cebd2b97b41#33]. Table 3 likewise labels the class+distillation row as the late fusion of the class and distillation classifiers [S:4cebd2b97b41#40].

citations.text:
D.3
HEAD TYPE AND CLASS TOKEN
In order to stay as close as possible to the original Transformer model, we made use of an additional
[class] token, which is taken as image representation. The output of this token is then trans-
formed into a class prediction via a small multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with tanh as non-linearity
in the single hidden layer.

However, we found that this is neither due to the extra token, nor to the GAP operation. Instead,

citations.title: arXiv:2012.12877v2  [cs.CV]  15 Jan 2021
citations.text:
The class token
is a trainable vector, appended to the patch tokens before the
ﬁrst layer, that goes through the transformer layers, and is then projected with
a linear layer to predict the class. This class token is inherited from NLP [14],
and departs from the typical pooling layers used in computer vision to predict
the class. The transformer thus process batches of (N + 1) tokens of dimension
D, of which only the class vector is used to predict the output. This architecture
forces the self-attention to spread information between the patch tokens and
the class token: at training time the supervision signal comes only from the
class embedding, while the patch tokens are the model’s only variable input.

As mentioned earlier, our architecture design is identical to the one proposed
by Dosovitskiy et al. [15] with no convolutions. Our only differences are the
training strategies, and the distillation token. Also we do not use a MLP head
for the pre-training but only a linear classiﬁer. To avoid any confusion, we refer
to the results obtained in the prior work by ViT, and preﬁx ours by DeiT. If not
speciﬁed, DeiT refers to our referent model DeiT-B, which has the same archi-
tecture as ViT-B. When we ﬁne-tune DeiT at a larger resolution, we append the
resulting operating resolution at the end, e.g, DeiT-B↑384. Last, when using
our distillation procedure, we identify it with an alembic sign as DeiT⚗.

citations.title: arXiv:2012.12877v2  [cs.CV]  15 Jan 2021
citations.text:
Distillation token.
We now focus on our proposal, which is illustrated in
Figure 2. We add a new token, the distillation token, to the initial embeddings
(patches and class token). Our distillation token is used similarly as the class
token: it interacts with other embeddings through self-attention, and is output
by the network after the last layer. Its target objective is given by the distillation
component of the loss. The distillation embedding allows our model to learn
from the output of the teacher, as in a regular distillation, while remaining
complementary to the class embedding.
Interestingly, we observe that the learned class and distillation tokens con-

At test time, both the
class or the distillation embeddings produced by the transformer are associ-
ated with linear classiﬁers and able to infer the image label. Yet our referent
method is the late fusion of these two separate heads, for which we add the
softmax output by the two classiﬁers to make the prediction. We evaluate these
three options in Section 5.
